awd_titl_txt: I-Corps: Translation Potential of Machine Learning to Optimize Polymer Nanocomposite Solutions for Thermal Management and Moisture Protection
awd_abstract_narration:
This I-Corps project focusses on the commercialization of a software solution to optimize the selection of materials used to design and develop solar panels. Software solutions have the potential to significantly enhance the efficiency and longevity of solar panels by preventing overheating, which is a critical challenge in the solar energy sector. Rapid and accurate material selection can also be applied to other industries requiring thermal management solutions, including rechargeable batteries, semiconductors, and electronics. The increasing demand for improved energy efficiency, coupled with the scalability of the software, could offer a more cost-effective solution for improving the functionality, reliability and durability of solar panels, energy storage devices, and other electronics.

This I-Corps project utilizes experiential learning coupled with a first-hand investigation of the industry ecosystem to assess the translation potential of a proprietary machine learning (ML) algorithm to identify, design, develop, and synthesize polymer nanocomposites. These materials address critical challenges in thermal management and barrier protection for a range of industries, including solar, rechargeable batteries, semiconductors, and supercapacitors. By utilizing machine learning modeling for material classification, the design, development, and selection of materials with the desired properties is accelerated. These nanocomposites may reduce infrared absorption, provide UV shielding, and perform as a barrier against oxygen, moisture, and other contamination, improving the functionality, reliability, and durability of solar panels.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
NJIT and Materium Technologies participated in the NSF National I-Corps program to test if the team's advanced polymer nanocomposite technology can solve a real and urgent market problem. At the start of the project, the team believed the strongest opportunity was in solar energy. The initial hypothesis was that engineers would use machine learning-assisted material selection to develop thermal management layers for solar panels, with the goal of reducing overheating and improving panel performance and lifetime.

Through the National I-Corps process, the team conducted more than 100 customer discovery interviews and attended 9 industry events with people working across solar, batteries, microelectronics, semiconductor packaging, photonics, sensors, coatings, manufacturing, and advanced materials. These interviews helped the team move from a broad technical platform to a more focused commercialization path.

The most important finding was that the original solar panel market was not the best initial beachhead. Solar manufacturers are highly cost-sensitive, and their purchasing decisions are driven mainly by cost per watt, not by a standalone materials improvement unless the return on investment is immediate and clearly proven. The team also learned that customers were not strongly interested in a standalone machine learning software product for materials discovery. Instead, customers cared more about validated physical materials that could be integrated into their existing manufacturing process.

The project helped the team identify a stronger initial market in protective coatings for microelectronics and semiconductor packaging. Customer discovery showed that engineers in these markets face recurring problems with moisture damage, corrosion, electrical leakage, delamination, and difficulty protecting smaller and more complex electronic devices. The team also learned that customers want coatings that are thin, flexible, reliable, electrically insulating, compatible with existing deposition tools, and easier to rework or repair than some current high-performance coating options.

These findings sharpened the intellectual merit of our technology. The team’s updated core scientific and technical hypothesis is that a self-assembling polymer nanocomposite coating can form highly ordered nanoscale layers in a simpler wet coating process, creating a multifunctional protective coating for electronics. The I-Corps interviews clarified which technical metrics matter most to future customers, including dielectric strength, moisture protection, coating thickness, flexibility, adhesion, crack resistance, thermal tolerance, process compatibility, and reliability under humidity and temperature stress. This customer input now guides the next stage of experiments, testing, and prototype development.

The broader impacts of the project are also clearer. If successfully developed, this coating could help extend the life of electronic devices, reduce failures caused by moisture and corrosion, lower e-waste, and support more reliable products in consumer, industrial, and defense-related applications. A coating that can be applied using simpler equipment and potentially repaired or recycled reduces manufacturing complexity and also supports more sustainable electronics production. This also strengthened the team’s ability to translate laboratory research into a product guided by real customer needs.

As a result of the NSF National I-Corps, the team changed its commercialization strategy. The next steps are to continue follow-up discussions with end users (process and manufacturing engineers) and decision makers, test the non-functional coating MVP, build the prototype based on customer learning, compare performance against incumbent coatings, and pursue non-dilutive funding (NSF SBIR) to reduce technical and market risk. The team will prioritize joint development discussions with early adopters, including electronics manufacturers, contract manufacturers, and semiconductor packaging groups. The long-term goal is to move from customer discovery to prototype validation, reliability testing, pilot-scale coating, and eventually a scalable business model for advanced protective coatings.
